rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taghābun warns that love of wife and children can become a trial: it may make a person shirk spending his life and wealth for God and turn family friendship into self-harm.
rows.anchor: because of his intense love for them, he starts to evade spending his life and wealth for the cause of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vigilance does not require severing family ties; one should forgive and forbear as far as possible, reforming relatives while protecting oneself from harm.
rows.anchor: he should, on the contrary, be as much forgiving and foregoing in their matter as is possible for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭalāq sets limits for a husband who hates his wife, while the following al-Taḥrīm explains limits in situations of love; neither emotion excuses excess against God’s law.
rows.anchor: if for some reason, a person starts to hate his wife, then how he should observe limits set by God in her matter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because marriage is foundational and emotions can lead people to violate sharīʿah limits, the two sūrahs explain Taghābun and warn that such excess leads to humiliation in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: this sūrah and the next are merely an explanation of what is concisely stated in Sūrah al-Taghābun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct address to the Prophet concerns his role as Muslim leader and trustee, not his person; the directives therefore carry special weight for the community.
rows.anchor: it relates to his status as the leader and trustee of the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the addressed abuses were widespread in pre-Islamic Arabia, God directly instructs the Prophet; if even he must obey, the directives are essential for everyone.
rows.anchor: when the Prophet (sws) too is told to obey them, then it it becomes essential for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–7 prohibit immediately expelling a wife after pronouncing divorce and require the prescribed procedure regardless of the husband’s wealth or poverty.
rows.anchor: it is not lawful to expel one’s wife from the house immediately by uttering the divorce sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who observe God’s limits despite financial hardship to please Him receive special aid; those who violate them from greed only wrong themselves.
rows.anchor: People, who, in spite of their financial difficulties, set out to observe the limits set by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 8–12 warn that nations disobeying God and His messengers have been punished; Muslims should honor the Prophet’s guidance to attain Paradise, remembering God’s sovereign power.
rows.anchor: all those nations who had disobeyed God and His Prophets have always been severely punished by Him

none: Bare sūrah title and copyright notice only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qalam pairs with al-Mulk: both warn Quraysh of judgment and worldly consequences for denial, but al-Qalam uses a sterner tone and different arguments.
rows.anchor: the difference lies in the style, nature of arguments and the tone adopted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following al-Mulk’s closing challenge, al-Qalam compares the Prophet’s preaching, Book, and character with Quraysh’s corrupt leadership to show that the guided will succeed and their leaders lead them to ruin.
rows.anchor: a comparison is made in this sūrah between the preaching of the Prophet (sws), the Book presented by him and his lofty character

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard parable warns Quraysh that present peace and blessings do not last: God can remove them suddenly and leave people to face the consequences.
rows.anchor: the peace and security they have today should not mislead them to think that they would remain under the same conditions forever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah rebukes those who assume they will receive worldly favors in the Hereafter and challenges them to produce a divine scripture or binding oath for that claim; God does not equate righteous and wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: they are asked how they have regarded God to be so unjust that He would equate the righteous with the wrongdoers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hereafter challenge asks disbelievers to prove their claimed entitlement through scripture, oath, or guarantors, while assuring the Prophet that their delusion will be exposed.
rows.anchor: if they have any oath from God in this regard or if there are some people who have assured them of this, then they should present this evidence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has trapped these opponents in the long respite He grants; the Prophet should await God’s decision without imitating Jonah’s impatience and resulting trial.
rows.anchor: these people have been caught in the long noose of the respite given to them by God

none: Verse translation only; no separate exegetical point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As with Qāf at 50:1, Nūn is named in the opening; Arabic syntax suppresses the inchoative, supplied in the translation as “This is Sūrah Nūn.”
rows.anchor: According to linguistic principles of Arabic, the mubtatadā’ (inchoative) is suppressed here

rows.speaker: Imām Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī holds that the disjointed letters are names of their sūrahs used to signify meaning, though most meanings have been lost.
rows.anchor: According to him, these are names of their respective sūrahs and are used to signify some meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn still means fish; its use alludes to Jonah, called the companion of the fish at the sūrah’s end and dhū al-nūn in al-Anbiyāʾ.
rows.anchor: the allusion is to the Prophet Jonah (sws) who had been swallowed by a fish

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw is an oath, and Qur’anic oaths substantiate claims; here the oath supports three opening claims, beginning with the opponents’ folly in calling the Prophet possessed.
rows.anchor: such oaths are meant to substantiate a claim(s).

rows.speaker: Muj āhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid reports that the pen is the one used to write the Qur’an and “what they write” refers to the Qur’an itself.
rows.anchor: there is a narrative from Muj āhid that the word “pen” refers to the pen with which

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Writing is a divine favor that safeguards revelation from the corruption and loss that threatened earlier oral teachings; scripture was written, and the Qur’an was preserved against alteration.
rows.anchor: In order to protect religion from this danger, the Almighty taught man the use of the pen and writing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the author’s view, the pen oath means the written record of divine teachings, including earlier scriptures whose testimony supports Muhammad’s prophethood and advent.
rows.anchor: it refers to all the written record of divine teachings which was preserved through the pen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Context identifies “what they write” as the Qur’an being revealed and recorded by the Companions; its elevated discourse attests to Muhammad’s truthfulness, civility, and prophethood.
rows.anchor: which was being revealed at that time and was being written by the Companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by earlier scriptures and the Qur’an completes the claim that Muhammad is not possessed but teaches the same message as prophets from Adam to Jesus, whose truth history confirms.
rows.anchor: he is, in fact, imparting to people the same teachings as were imparted by all other prophets of God from Adam (sws) to Jesus (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh called Muhammad mad because they could not understand his certainty about impending punishment and saw his anxious, compassionate preaching influencing people; they alleged hallucination and magic to discredit him.
rows.anchor: their leaders were totally unable to understand from where the punishment with which he was emphatically and vehemently warning them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 3 reverses the opponents’ expectation: the Prophet has unending reward, while arrogant opponents face imminent punishment and devastation.
rows.anchor: for the Prophet (sws), there is an everlasting reward; these arrogant people whose affluence has made them proud

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ghayr means “unending”; alternative interpretations conflict with Arabic usage and parallel Qur’anic verses.
rows.anchor: means “unending.” Some people have interpreted it differently; however, this interpretation is not only against linguistic principles of Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s lofty character, like that of earlier prophets, answers those who dismiss his mission as poetry, soothsaying, or madness.
rows.anchor: just as prophets before him had exemplary character, he too, has a lofty character

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an contrasts the Prophet with poets and soothsayers whose morals, reasoning, and practice are degraded; those grouping him with them are rebuked.
rows.anchor: the moral depletion of poets and soothsayers, their intellectual ramblings and the lack of correspondence between what they claim and what they practice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The approaching judgment distinguishes believers led by the Prophet from Quraysh led by Abū Lahab and Abū Jahl; it reveals who Satan led astray and who was guided to success in both worlds.
rows.anchor: the believers who are led by the Prophet (sws), or the Quraysh are who led by Abū Lahab and Abū Jahal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s messengers decide their nations’ fate in this world as well as the Hereafter; this repeats al-Mulk’s closing warning.
rows.anchor: the messengers of God decide the fate of their respective nations in this very world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maftūn means one led astray by the world and Satan, not simply a mad person; those led this way are truly mad and lead their followers to Hell.
rows.anchor: It connotes its original meaning, ie. a person who has been led away by this world and by Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fully knows who is guided and who deviates, and will judge each accordingly; the watched world must culminate in judgment so the righteous and wrongdoers are not treated alike.
rows.anchor: It is essential that it culminate in a Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God’s wisdom and justice will ultimately manifest, the Prophet should ignore deniers of resurrection who imagine they would keep the same favors if it came.
rows.anchor: This world is not revolving around their desires; it has been created by a wise and powerful being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word iṭāʿah here means being affected or influenced, a usage found in both Qur’anic and classical Arabic.
rows.anchor: It is used in this sense in both the Qur’ān and in classical Arabic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents want Muhammad to soften his position so they can make reciprocal concessions; their opposition is bargaining against desire, not sincere commitment to religion.
rows.anchor: they have no doubt in the veracity of what he says; however, accepting it is against their desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s syntax suppresses the inchoative; the full sense is “they too will soften,” after the Prophet softens his stance.
rows.anchor: it is their desire that the Prophet (sws) softens his stance and then they too will soften their attitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following warning is joined to the preceding one and describes the collective Quraysh leadership, not a particular person; it contrasts their degradation with the Prophet’s character.
rows.anchor: The verse does not refer to someone in particular, as has been generally understood by people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corrupt traits characterize Quraysh leaders such as Abū Lahab, Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, Abū Jahl, and Akhnas ibn Shurayq; the generic wording and later plural support a group reading.
rows.anchor: the character of such leaders of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥallāf means one who swears frequently and is never positive; paired with “despicable,” it depicts a person lacking self-respect and relying on oaths from insecurity.
rows.anchor: this word never comes in the positive sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites swear to disguise their character; Quraysh leaders, unable to find fault or argue against Islam, swore that Muhammad was a poet, soothsayer, madman, or liar.
rows.anchor: The only means they had to fool their masses was to swear profusely

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hammaz is an emphatic form meaning maker of evil gestures; mockers use bodily signs, facial movements, and words to belittle others, as Quraysh did to Muhammad and poor Muslims.
rows.anchor: Making such evil gestures and verbal caricatures is a special trait of those who want to belittle someone in the eyes of others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh used backbiting and rumor-mongering to sow discord and disgruntlement, undermine Islam’s fraternity, and divide Muslims; the arrogant turn to such tactics when argument fails.
rows.anchor: they were vehemently engaged in spreading rumours and misconceptions among Muslims in order to cause dissension between them
